# Gauss-localized support variations preserving every active compatibility

This is an all-dimensional necessary-condition theorem for a smooth
positive-curvature local minimum. It does not assume strict anchored
compatibility. It extends the first-order part of the archived planar
support-arc mechanism by using only affine-in-base perturbations, which
preserve ALL compatibility gaps exactly. It does not regularize a general
minimum or supply a numerical OC bound.

## 1. Setting

Let d>=2 and let P be a finite subset of R^n. At each p in P let K_p
be a positive d-dimensional convex body with support function h_p on
the unit sphere S^(d-1). Assume h_p is C2 and its spherical curvature
matrix

    Q_p(u)=Hess_S h_p(u)+h_p(u) I_(u-perpendicular)

is positive definite for every u. The finite family is actual, meaning

    sum_p alpha_p K_p subset K_q

for every anchored convex representation q=sum_p alpha_p p in P.
Equivalently h_q(u)>=sum_p alpha_p h_p(u) for every u. The original
gaps may be zero on arbitrary closed sets of directions.

The inverse Gauss map and surface-area density are

    x_p(u)=grad_S h_p(u)+h_p(u)u,
    J_p(u)=det Q_p(u)>0.

Thus a surface integral on boundary K_p equals the spherical integral
with density J_p. The identity follows by differentiating x_p in a
tangent direction: its tangential derivative is Q_p. The exterior
normal is u, so the tangential Jacobian is det Q_p. Positive definiteness
gives the usual one-to-one regular Gauss parametrization.

Use mu=sum_p vol_d on the finite union of fibers and M=mu(S). Let beta
be its maximum normalized closed-halfspace depth. Suppose this family
is a local minimum among ALL nearby positive actual families on P.
Only the explicit perturbations below will be needed from that hypothesis.

## 2. Signed Gauss-localized affine-base variations are actual

Choose arbitrary C2 functions psi_0,...,psi_n on the sphere and put

    delta h_p(u)=psi_0(u)+sum_(l=1)^n p_l psi_l(u).

For sufficiently small positive AND negative t, every h_p+t delta h_p
is the support function of a positive convex body K_p(t). Indeed the
smallest eigenvalues of the finitely many Q_p have a common positive
lower bound on the compact sphere. The C2 perturbations preserve
positive definiteness for small |t|. Widths and interior balls also
remain positive. For completeness, the one-homogeneous extension of
each perturbed h has positive-semidefinite Hessian off zero: its
tangential Hessian is Q/|x| and its radial Hessian is zero. The positive
width gives the correct one-sided derivative order on a line passing
through zero. Restrictions to all other lines are convex by their
nonnegative second derivative. Hence the extension is convex and is
a support function. Uniformly small support changes keep the bodies
bounded and their fixed smaller interior balls positive.

For every anchored representation the perturbation cancels EXACTLY:

    delta h_q-sum_p alpha_p delta h_p
       =psi_0(1-sum alpha_p)
          +sum_l psi_l(q_l-sum_p alpha_p p_l)=0.

Consequently every original compatibility gap, including every active
one, is unchanged at every normal. The new family is actual for both
signs of t. There is no uniform-slack argument and no assumption that
the active representation list is locally constant in u.

The body realizing it is the convex hull of the new fibers; the exact
support inclusions ensure its sections at P equal K_p(t). When P is
lattice-convex and is the full integer trace of its base projection,
this also retains precisely that integer base set. For a general
finite P the theorem concerns its specified measured fibers only.

## 3. First masses and every fixed cap

In the Gauss parametrization, the moving point has normal velocity
delta h_p(u). A bounded normal-graph displacement of a compact smooth
boundary changes volume to first order by its surface integral:
normal tubular coordinates have Jacobian1+O(displacement), uniformly,
so integrating their thin signed intervals proves the formula. Thus

    M'(0)=sum_p int_S delta h_p(u) J_p(u) du.           (1)

Write a fixed nonvertical ambient cap as

    H={ (p,x):a dot p+v dot x>=b }, |v|=1.

A proper cutting hyperplane meets a strictly convex smooth boundary
in a surface-null set; a supporting hyperplane meets it in a singleton,
also surface-null because d>=2. The Gauss map preserves this null-set
property since its Jacobians are continuous and bounded away from zero.
Away from this null set the cap indicator is constant on the small
normal displacement interval. A uniform velocity bound and dominated
convergence give

    (mu_t(H))'(0)
      =sum_p int_S delta h_p(u) J_p(u)
                     1_H(p,x_p(u)) du.                (2)

Both derivatives exist from both signs. Proper section areas are
continuous in the cap threshold. Their limits at supporting thresholds
are zero, because strict convexity excludes a positive-area support
facet. Hence all selected critical caps have equal left and right
threshold slopes S_H>0, the strict positivity coming from their
proper section through the interior of an anchor fiber.

## 4. One common pointwise stress for any selected critical cover

Choose one finite positive critical circuit at each deepest base, or
any finite collection of complete such groups covering all deepest
bases. Denote their caps H_ij, continuous normals v_ij, and positive
weights rho_ij with sum_j rho_ij v_ij=0. Every selected cap has mass
Q=beta M. Fixed slack circuit covers are retained at other bases.
The existence and whole-fiber coverage of these finite circuits are
the previously proved critical-cap lemmas; no finite representation
of the full depth function, sharp center, or unique center is assumed.

Put

    kappa_ij=(rho_ij/S_ij)/(sum_j rho_ij/S_ij),
    c_i(p,u)=sum_j kappa_ij 1_(H_ij)(p,x_p(u)).

For a perturbation delta h the i-th normalized circuit response, apart
from the common positive factor1/M, is

    A_i(delta h)
       =sum_p int_S delta h_p J_p(c_i(p,u)-beta)du.    (3)

To verify this directly, let g_ij be the cap mass derivative in(2),
and let L_i=sum_j kappa_ij g_ij. Shift cap thresholds by
t(g_ij-L_i)/S_ij. Their rho-weighted sum of shifts is zero, preserving
the original projected whole-fiber cover exactly. Each cap then has
mass Q+tL_i+o(t). If all A_i were negative, the selected covers would
bound every deepest fiber strictly below beta times the new total
mass. All other finitely many covers keep their strict gap. This
would be a genuine decrease of full maximum depth.

Thus no signed perturbation in Section2 has all A_i negative. Its
image under A is a linear subspace of a finite-dimensional real
space. Separating this subspace from the open negative orthant gives

    pi_i>=0, sum_i pi_i=1,
    sum_i pi_i A_i(delta h)=0 for EVERY tuple(psi_0,...,psi_n).

The equality follows because both signs of every perturbation are
available. Define lambda_ij=pi_i kappa_ij/beta. These are independent
of u and sum to1/beta. Testing each arbitrary smooth psi_l yields
the pointwise identities, for almost every u,

    sum_p J_p(u)[1-sum_(i,j)lambda_ij
                     1_(H_ij)(p,x_p(u))] (1,p)=0.     (4)

The vector(1,p) retains the mass equation and ALL affine base moments
simultaneously. Smooth test functions determine integrable densities,
so this passage does not presume pointwise differentiability of cap
indicators. On every open region where their finite incidence pattern
is constant, the left side is continuous and (4) holds everywhere.

The same lambda handles all Gauss-localized affine-base perturbations
for the chosen cover. Different selections of critical covers can
give different lambda. A local minimum must admit (4) for EVERY such
selection. Discarding that quantifier would lose the information
demonstrated by the exact simplex roof obstruction.

## 5. Exact crossing equations and an affine-separation test

Let u(s) be a smooth spherical arc with u(0)=u_* such that, for each
small nonzero s, no selected cap boundary is met by any x_p(u(s)),
and each incidence is constant separately for s>0 and s<0. Define

    Delta_(ij,p)=1_(H_ij)(p,x_p(u(0+)))
                  -1_(H_ij)(p,x_p(u(0-))) in{-1,0,1}.

Taking the two limits in(4) and using continuity of J_p gives

    sum_(p,i,j) lambda_ij Delta_(ij,p) J_p(u_*) (1,p)=0. (5)

The incidence limits, rather than membership at the crossing point,
are used. Closed-boundary mass has not been dropped: it is null for
these surface integrals and was retained in the exact cap covers.

In particular, an isolated crossing of one cap at one fiber forces
that cap's multiplier to vanish. More generally let P_+ be the bases
of positive jumps and P_- the bases of negative jumps. If their
convex hulls are disjoint, every cap having a nonzero jump must have
zero multiplier. Indeed a strictly separating affine function ell
is positive on P_+ and negative on P_-. Pairing(5) with its affine
coefficient vector makes every nonzero-jump summand nonnegative and
strictly positive when its cap multiplier is positive. If one sign
set is empty, the mass coordinate alone gives the same conclusion.

Therefore a finite collection of such crossing events that includes
at least one cap of every selected group contradicts local minimality:
kappa_ij>0 makes its vanishing lambda imply pi_i=0, whereas sum pi_i=1.
This is a concrete sufficient descent obstruction with an explicit
geometric incidence criterion, not an assertion that the criterion
always holds.

## 6. Remaining boundaries of the result

Active compatibility is fully allowed in Sections1--5. Positive C2
curvature, however, is an explicit hypothesis and has not been obtained
by smoothing a general minimum. Flat facets, singular curvature, or
degenerating support Hessians require different feasible variations.
The archived planar diffuse-curvature results treat some such issues
in dimension2 but do not automatically yield this all-dimensional
regularization.

The crossing equation can be satisfied by opposite incidence changes
on different fibers with intersecting base convex hulls. Neither
common curvature nor log-concavity alone has been shown to prevent
those cancellations. A proof that enough separating crossings must
occur at a below-target minimum is not supplied. This is the precise
new geometric task, not a completed OC proof or a disguised assertion
that a generic configuration may replace an attained minimum.

## 7. Common nonlinear normal changes also preserve compatibility

Let H_p be the one-homogeneous support extension and let Z(u) be any
C2 vector field with values in R^d. For small signed t put

    h_p(t,u)=H_p(u+tZ(u)).

The argument never evaluates H_p at zero. These functions converge in
C2 to h_p, so their curvature matrices and widths stay positive.
They are support functions by the argument in Section2. Every anchored
compatibility inequality remains true because all H_p are evaluated at
the SAME vector u+tZ(u). The first support velocity is

    delta h_p(u)=x_p(u) dot Z(u).                    (7)

This is not asserted to be a nonlinear map of the physical body or of
the mixed lattice. It is a direct construction of new support functions
whose convexity and compatibility have been checked separately.

Signed affine-base additions from Section2 can be made simultaneously:
add t[psi_0(u)+sum p_l psi_l(u)] after the common evaluation. Their
compatibility contributions still cancel exactly. Thus a single
separation over the enlarged linear first-variation space supplies a
single collection lambda satisfying both(4) and

    sum_p J_p(u)[1-sum_(i,j)lambda_ij
                       1_(H_ij)(p,x_p(u))] x_p(u)=0. (8)

Together these are the pointwise full boundary-point moment equation
with vector(1,p,x_p(u)). In(5) the jump equation may consequently also
use this longer vector. The sufficient separation test then separates
the actual full boundary points(p,x_p(u_*)), not just their bases.

## 8. Concave support-value contractions give pointwise convex order

The same lambda can be required to satisfy a stronger condition. Let
psi>=0 be C2 on the sphere and let phi(z,s) be a smooth convex function
on a neighborhood of the compact ranges in question. For epsilon>=0
small, define

    h'_p(u)=h_p(u)-epsilon psi(u) phi(p,h_p(u)).       (9)

This is an actual one-sided perturbation even at active compatibility.
For fixed u the function

    F_u(z,s)=s-epsilon psi(u)phi(z,s)

is concave jointly in(z,s) and increasing in s on the bounded range,
because its s derivative remains positive for sufficiently small
epsilon. If q=sum alpha_p p and h_q>=sum alpha_p h_p, then

    F_u(q,h_q)>=F_u(q,sum alpha_p h_p)
                  >=sum alpha_p F_u(p,h_p).

This is exactly the perturbed support compatibility inequality.
The support functions remain C2-close, hence have positive curvature
and are genuine positive-body support functions. Both the sign and
the monotonicity condition in this construction are essential.

Any finite nonnegative sum of the contractions(9) is realized by
F_u(z,s)=s-sum_a epsilon_a psi_a(u)phi_a(z,s). It can be combined
with the signed affine additions and common normal changes in Section7
by applying F_u AFTER those operations. For sufficiently small
parameters the full composition remains increasing and concave in
the scalar support value. Its first velocity is the sum of the listed
velocities. This proves feasibility of the entire first-variation
cone used next, rather than presuming that individually feasible
directions can be added.

Apply finite-dimensional separation to its response cone in R^k,
exactly as in the roof argument. There is one pi>=0 of sum1 for which
sum_i pi_i A_i>=0 on this cone, with equality on its signed linear
part. Consequently the same lambda has(4),(8), and

    sum_p J_p(u)[1-sum_(i,j)lambda_ij
        1_(H_ij)(p,x_p(u))] phi(p,h_p(u))>=0           (10)

for every smooth convex phi and every u outside the finite cap-crossing
sets. To justify this pointwise assertion, fix phi and use arbitrary
nonnegative localized psi in(9). On any open incidence region the
integrand is continuous. A negative value would persist on a small
open set and contradict the integral inequality. This argument applies
separately to any phi at any such u, so no intersection of uncountably
many measure-one sets is needed.

Finite maxima of affine functions are also allowed as tests in(10).
Approximate max_l ell_l uniformly by
epsilon log(sum_l exp(ell_l/epsilon)); its error is between0 and
epsilon log(number of terms). These are smooth convex functions,
and the finite sums in(10) pass to the limit.

Fix such a regular u and put

    w_p=(p,h_p(u)),
    mu_p=J_p(u),
    nu_p=J_p(u)sum_(i,j)lambda_ij 1_(H_ij)(p,x_p(u)).

These nonnegative finite measures have the same total mass and the
same first moment in w. The mass and base moments follow from(4);
the h moment follows from(8) by pairing with u. Equation(10) says
nu is dominated by mu in convex order on this finite support.

## 9. Finite transport proof and its lift to actual boundary points

Here is an elementary finite version of the required convex-order
transport statement. If weights nu_p,mu_q on finite points w_p obey
the preceding convex inequalities, then there are numbers T_pq>=0
such that

    sum_q T_pq=nu_p,
    sum_p T_pq=mu_q,
    sum_q T_pq w_q=nu_p w_p.                         (11)

Proof: consider all nonnegative arrays satisfying the row mass and
row barycenter conditions, and let K be their possible column-mass
vectors. This is a nonempty compact convex polytope: the diagonal
array is feasible. If mu were outside K, strict separation would give
real numbers b_q with

    sum_q b_q mu_q<min_(m in K) sum_q b_q m_q.

Let f be the convex lower envelope of the data(w_q,b_q) on their
convex hull. Explicitly,

    f(w)=min{sum_q alpha_q b_q:
              alpha_q>=0, sum alpha_q=1, sum alpha_q w_q=w}.

This is a continuous piecewise affine convex function on that hull,
represented there by finitely many affine minorants. The minimization
over rows gives the right side above as sum_p nu_p f(w_p). But convex
order and f(w_q)<=b_q imply

    sum_p nu_p f(w_p)<=sum_q mu_q f(w_q)<=sum_q mu_q b_q,

a contradiction. This proves(11). Zero row weights cause no problem.

Every positive row in(11) is an anchored equality

    p=sum_q (T_pq/nu_p)q,
    h_p(u)=sum_q (T_pq/nu_p)h_q(u).

Keep these coefficients fixed while changing the normal variable.
The compatibility gap h_p(v)-sum_q(T_pq/nu_p)h_q(v) is everywhere
nonnegative and equals zero at u. Its spherical gradient at u is
therefore zero. Combining its zero value and gradient gives

    x_p(u)=sum_q (T_pq/nu_p)x_q(u).                  (12)

Thus the SAME array transports the weighted cap-incidence measure
to the surface-area measure while preserving the full actual boundary
point(p,x_p(u)) in every row. The transport is supported on actual
active anchored compatibility equalities. It is not an invented
coupling of unrelated fiber centroids.

This proves, in particular, convex order on the full finite boundary
point set: for every convex Phi(z,x), apply Jensen to(11),(12) and
sum the rows. In the strictly compatible case only identity rows are
possible, so nu_p=mu_p separately at every p. With active compatibility,
nonidentity rows are explicitly retained instead of being discarded.

The construction is pointwise in a normal. No measurable choice of T
as u varies has been asserted, and no integral involving T is used
here. Such a choice, or a simultaneous transport across several cap
directions, would require an additional proof. Nor does this lemma
turn the boundary transport into a global cap-mass inequality with
constant Gamma_d. It is a precise all-dimensional constraint beyond
the affine shared-plane moments, with its stated curvature hypothesis.

## 10. A measurable choice and an integrated boundary coupling

The pointwise transports can in fact be selected measurably; no general
measurable-selection theorem is needed. Let U be the open full-measure
set of normals outside the finite selected cap-boundary preimages.
On U the weights and points in(11) are continuous on each incidence
region and Borel globally. Use the full points(p,x_p(u)) in the linear
system(11), which is feasible by(12). Flatten its nonnegative variables
T_pq into a vector t and write that finite system as

    A(u)t=b(u), t>=0.

Its coefficients are Borel; all entries apart from the incidence
weights are continuous. Every feasible set is a nonempty bounded
polytope, because every entry is bounded by its specified row mass.
It therefore has a vertex. At such a vertex the columns corresponding
to strictly positive entries are linearly independent: otherwise a
nonzero kernel vector supported there would allow a small perturbation
in both signs, contradicting extremality. Extend those columns, if
necessary, to rank A(u) independent columns, inserting zero entries
on the added columns. Some equally sized row minor is invertible.

Enumerate once and for all the finitely many choices of a rank, row
minor, and column subset, in a fixed order. For each choice define the
candidate basic vector by inverting its square minor and setting all
other entries zero. Test that its minor is nonzero, that the chosen
rank equals rank A(u), that t>=0, and that ALL the original equations
hold. These are Borel tests: rank is specified by finitely many zero
and nonzero minors, and each candidate is rational in the Borel matrix
entries where its determinant is nonzero. The preceding vertex argument
guarantees at least one feasible candidate. Selecting the first such
candidate gives a Borel array T_pq(u) on U. Set it to zero on the
excluded null set. It is integrable because row masses are bounded
by a fixed multiple of the continuous J_p on the compact sphere.

Define two finite measures on the actual fiber boundaries by

    dmu_boundary(p,x_p(u))=J_p(u)du,
    dnu_boundary(p,x_p(u))=nu_p(u)du.

The array T_pq(u)du is a coupling from nu_boundary to mu_boundary
that retains the SAME normal u and has row barycenter equal to the
full input boundary point(p,x_p(u)). More explicitly, its column
and row marginal identities follow by integrating(11), and for every
Borel set of input normals its first-moment identity follows by
integrating(12) over that set. Thus it supplies the usual conditional
barycenter property without requiring a disintegration theorem.

For any continuous convex function Phi on the ambient space, apply
finite Jensen in each row and integrate. All terms are bounded on
the compact boundary union, and finite sums commute with the integral.
This gives the fully integrated necessary condition

    int Phi dnu_boundary<=int Phi dmu_boundary,
    nu_boundary=sum_(i,j)lambda_ij
                         (mu_boundary restricted to H_ij).   (13)

Their masses and full first moments are equal. The chosen transport
uses only actual active anchored representations, with their continuous
boundary-point equalities, at every regular normal. Exceptional normals
have zero surface measure, and no assertion about their selected row
weights is needed for(13).

This closes the measurable-choice issue for the PRESENT pointwise
transport. It does not make transports from different selected critical
covers agree, does not turn boundary area into uniform fiber volume,
and does not choose a deterministic mixed-integer center with the OC
constant. Those are separate obligations of any subsequent argument.
